new_statements.quote: p. 578: "A characteristic of the language is a strong stress-accent, noted by me often as a long vowel, and by G. Morgenstierne with an accent mark. All vowels can be reduced to ə when unaccented, and w and y are often reduced to ᵘ or ⁱ or dropped. Unvoicing of final consonants is also not uncommon." p. 568: "a) Words accented differently in Wan and Pš: angīn 'honey' — Pš gabīna; or- 'there' in compounds, < ávaθra-; — Pš war- < aváθra-; kubīr 'pigeon' — Pš kautar; awlūn 'bridle' — Pš mlūn (but cf. Waz. wlīn)"

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Wanetsi with an empty rule. This source adds that a strong stress-accent exists, with schwa reduction of unaccented vowels, and that accent placement is word-specific (differs from Pashto cognates); it gives no placement rule, so it cannot agree with or contradict a catalog rule, only refine the empty record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Waṇetsi has a strong stress-accent (Elfenbein often wrote it as vowel length, Morgenstierne with an accent mark); unaccented vowels reduce to schwa. No positional or weight rule is given anywhere in the article; the placement is word-specific and can differ from the Pashto cognate (p. 568 item (a)), and the accented texts carry the mark on varying syllables, so the best label is lexical (mobile, unpredictable) stress as in Pashto, but the source itself states no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the texts are said to be un-normalised and 'in a rather fluid state', full of Pashto and Urdu material (p. 578).
new_statements.identity_note: Elfenbein 1967's texts are Waṇetsi of the Harnai and Čauter (Chauter) area of Balochistan (speakers named as Sayyid Sardar Šāh, Harnai, and Mullah Sayyid Mohammed, Čauter). Elfenbein 1997 is a chapter on Pashto phonology; whether it treats Waṇetsi at all, and as a dialect or a separate language, could not be checked.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed (Elfenbein 1997, not opened); Second spot-check: Hallberg 1992 (SSNP vol. 4, held by the project as, marked silent) -- confirmed silent on Waneci stress: the WaNeci chapter (pp. 45-52) says nothing about stress; the Appendix B word list gives 68 WCI rows and none carries the stress mark, while 54 of the Pashto PES rows do (so the absence is not a transcription convention); the only stress remarks are about Pashto (p. 15 n. 3 on unstressed ə, citing Skjaervo 1989:388; the Appendix A phonetic key). Small missed passage in Elfenbein 1967: p. 583, note 3 to the Translations and Notes, 'The accent marks indicate stress.' (supports the reader's statement; no new rule).
